anatomy.intro: Each peanut-shaped stem repeats a simple pattern of shallow ribs, small spine cushions, and side shoots.

parts.function: The green succulent stem stores water and captures light.
parts.label: Finger-shaped stem

parts.function: Longitudinal folds organize the expanding stem surface.
parts.label: Shallow rib

parts.function: Small cushions carry neat clusters of short spines.
parts.label: Areole

parts.function: A young side shoot helps the plant spread into a low clump.
parts.label: Basal offset

flowers.text: The peanut-cactus ancestor has funnel-shaped vermilion-red flowers 5–7 cm long. Hybrid flowers span a wider color palette, which makes the first open bloom especially interesting.

growth.note: The clump fills outward through offsets, so increasing spread can be more noticeable than increasing height.

stages.text: Short stems establish a compact starting group.
stages.title: Small cluster

stages.text: New fingers enlarge the plant sideways.
stages.title: Spreading offsets

stages.text: Mature stems can bear flowers much broader than the stems themselves.
stages.title: Flowering clump

habitat.text: Chamaelobivia hybrids combine peanut-cactus ancestry with other Echinopsis or Lobivia lines. The peanut-cactus ancestor, Echinopsis chamaecereus, comes from northwestern Argentina and grows as a low mat of slender, sprawling stems.

Probable Chamaelobivia peanut cactus hybrid: dense low cluster of short finger/peanut-shaped bright green stems, shallow ribs with neat white small radial spines. 1 points to a complete finger-like main stem; 2 to a shallow rib; 3 to a small areole bearing short spines; 4 to a tiny new basal offset. No flowers because cultivar is unknown.

lookalikes.name: Golden ball cactus
lookalikes.text: Parodia leninghausii develops a denser golden coat and an upright column; peanut hybrids spread as many fingerlike stems.

mature.text: Expect a low, spreading clump of many fingerlike stems. Hybrids vary in stem size and vigor.

milestones.text: Purchased at Carlsons' Greenhouse in a 4-inch individual pot.
milestones.title: Joined the collection

nameStory.text: The familiar peanut shape belongs to a species now listed by Kew as Echinopsis chamaecereus; Chamaecereus survives widely in horticultural hybrid names.
